cards.front: Why are 529 plans, LGIPs, and ABLE accounts regulated by the MSRB?
cards.back: All three are sponsored by state or local governments, making them municipal fund securities under MSRB jurisdiction.

A state-sponsored, tax-advantaged education savings account classified as a municipal fund security. Funds can be used for qualified K-12 expenses (up to $10,000/year) and qualified post-secondary expenses. Sales must be accompanied or preceded by an official statement/offering circular.

cards.front: What are the two basic types of 529 plans, and how do they differ?
cards.back: (1) Prepaid tuition plan — locks in current tuition rates at specific schools/systems for state residents; acts as a guaranteed inflation hedge. (2) College savings plan — allows contributions to be invested for later withdrawal for qualified education expenses at any eligible school; may or may not outpace inflation depending on performance.

cards.front: A parent is most concerned about rising tuition costs at a specific in-state university over the next 8 years. Which 529 option best hedges this risk?
cards.back: A 529 prepaid tuition plan. It locks in current tuition rates at the specific school/system, providing a guaranteed hedge against tuition inflation (the savings plan only might keep pace, depending on investment performance).

cards.front: How are 529 plan contributions and withdrawals treated for federal tax purposes?
cards.back: Contributions are made with after-tax dollars and are treated as gifts under federal tax law. Earnings grow tax-deferred. Withdrawals for qualified education expenses are tax-free federally. Nonqualified withdrawals are subject to income tax on earnings plus a 10% penalty.

cards.front: What tax disadvantage may exist if a client opens an out-of-state 529 plan?
cards.back: The client may lose state tax advantages such as state income tax deductions on contributions and/or tax-free withdrawals available only to in-state plan participants. Reps must disclose this to customers.

cards.front: If a 529 beneficiary receives a scholarship, what can the donor do without incurring the 10% penalty?
cards.back: The donor may withdraw an amount equal to the scholarship value penalty-free. Ordinary income tax on the earnings portion still applies.

cards.front: What happens if a 529 beneficiary does not use the funds for education?
cards.back: The donor can change the beneficiary to a family member of the original beneficiary with no tax consequences. Additionally, under SECURE 2.0 (effective 2024), unused funds may be rolled tax- and penalty-free to a Roth IRA for the beneficiary, subject to a $35,000 lifetime cap, a 15-year account age requirement, and the annual IRA contribution limit.

cards.front: Who controls the assets in a 529 plan, and are there income limits on contributors?
cards.back: The donor retains control of the account assets even after the beneficiary reaches legal age. There are no income limitations on contributors.

cards.front: How often may 529 plan assets be rolled over from one state's plan to another?
cards.back: No more than once every 12 months.

cards.front: Does the $10,000 annual qualified-expense limit on 529 plans apply to college costs?
cards.back: No. The $10,000 annual limit applies only to K-12 tuition. There is no $10,000 cap on qualified post-secondary expenses.

A trust established by a state to give other government entities (cities, counties, school districts, state agencies) a short-term investment vehicle. Participants buy shares/units of the pool's portfolio. Not a money market fund, but often operates similarly with a stable $1 NAV.

cards.front: Who are the investors in an LGIP?
cards.back: Other government entities (cities, counties, school districts, state agencies) — NOT retail investors.

cards.front: Are LGIPs required to register with the SEC?
cards.back: No. LGIPs fall within the governmental exemption, just like other municipal securities. There is no prospectus, but disclosure documents (information statement, investment policy, operating procedures) are provided. Oversight varies by state.

A tax-advantaged savings account, created by the ABLE Act of 2014, for individuals with significant disabilities whose disability onset occurred before age 26. The beneficiary is the account owner; earnings grow tax-free.

cards.front: Who is eligible to establish an ABLE account?
cards.back: An individual with a significant disability whose onset occurred before age 26. The beneficiary may currently be older than 26 — only the onset must have happened before age 26. Individuals already receiving SSI or SSDI who meet the age-onset criteria automatically qualify. Only one ABLE account per person is allowed.

cards.front: How are contributions to an ABLE account treated for federal tax purposes?
cards.back: Contributions are made with after-tax dollars and are NOT federally tax deductible. Anyone (the beneficiary, family, friends) may contribute. Total annual contributions are capped at a specified dollar amount (adjusted periodically for inflation). Earnings grow tax-free. Some states allow a state income tax deduction.

cards.front: A customer's nephew, the beneficiary of a 529 plan, receives a $15,000 athletic scholarship. Which of the following is NOT a permissible option? (a) Withdraw earnings up to the scholarship value tax-free; (b) Transfer the account to a sibling; (c) Withdraw $15,000 penalty-free; (d) Leave funds in the account.
cards.back: (a) is NOT permitted. The donor may withdraw up to the scholarship amount penalty-free, but ordinary income tax on earnings still applies — the withdrawal is not tax-free. Options (b), (c), and (d) are all permissible.

cards.front: Which regulator does NOT have jurisdiction over the structure or sale of 529 plans: SEC, IRS, MSRB, or Department of Education?
cards.back: Department of Education. The SEC (anti-fraud), IRS (tax treatment), and MSRB (rules governing sales of municipal fund securities) all have jurisdiction.
